meta.title: Arm Holdings: Rene Haas and the Architecture of Everything — How the World's Dominant CPU IP Licensor Is Converting Armv9 Royalty Leverage, Compute Subsystem Momentum, and a Historic Pivot into Physical Silicon to Build a Path Toward $25 Billion in Annual Revenue
meta.abstract:
Arm Holdings plc (NASDAQ: ARM) is the most consequential semiconductor intellectual property company in the world, licensing the CPU architectures that power an estimated 99 percent of smartphones, roughly half of all cloud data center cores added in 2025, and an expanding footprint across automotive, IoT, and AI inference hardware. Founded in 1990 as a joint venture between Acorn Computers, Apple Computer, and VLSI Technology, Arm built its durable competitive moat not by manufacturing chips but by collecting royalties and licensing fees on every silicon design that borrows its instruction set and core blueprints — a model that scales with the proliferation of connected devices rather than the capital cycles of fab construction.

The investment thesis centers on three compounding transitions under CEO Rene Haas, who took the helm in February 2022 and led the company through its $5.23 billion Nasdaq IPO in September 2023. First, the migration from Armv8 to Armv9 architecture commands royalty rates approximately double those of the prior generation; by Q4 fiscal 2025 (ended March 31, 2025), Armv9-based royalties had crossed 30 percent of total royalty income for the first time and continued accelerating through fiscal 2026. Second, Arm Compute Subsystems (CSS) — pre-integrated, production-ready chip blueprints sold to hyperscalers and OEMs — generate royalty rates double those of standalone core licenses, and by April 2026 Arm had signed 21 CSS licenses across 12 companies. Third, in March 2026 the company launched its first internally designed physical silicon, the Arm AGI CPU — a 3nm data center processor built for agentic AI workloads, with Meta as the lead partner and more than $2 billion in committed demand across fiscal years 2027 and 2028, signaling a structural expansion from pure IP licensor toward a vertically integrated platform company.

Fiscal year 2026 (ended March 31, 2026) delivered record total revenue of $4.92 billion, with royalty revenue of $2.61 billion (+21% year-over-year) and licensing revenue of $2.31 billion (+25%), against a backdrop of surging AI infrastructure spend from hyperscalers including Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and Meta. Data center royalties more than doubled year-over-year in Q4 fiscal 2026. SoftBank Group retains roughly 90 percent beneficial ownership, conferring strategic stability alongside governance concentration risk. A joint SoftBank-Arm roadmap presented in March 2026 targets $25 billion in annual revenue, implying a roughly 5x expansion from the fiscal 2026 base and validating the company's ambitions as the CPU foundation layer for the agentic AI era.

chapters.title: The Architecture of Everything: Arm's Strategic Position at the Dawn of the Agentic AI Era
chapters.body:
On March 24, 2026, Rene Haas stood before an audience of hyperscalers, cloud infrastructure operators, and AI platform companies to announce something that would have seemed paradoxical at any earlier point in Arm Holdings' thirty-five-year history: the company that had never manufactured a chip was now selling one. The Arm AGI CPU — a 3-nanometer data center processor built for agentic AI workloads — arrived with Meta as its lead development partner, OpenAI and Cloudflare as launch customers, and more than $2 billion in committed demand before a single production system had shipped. In the six weeks that followed, Arm's shares rose approximately 71 percent. The market was not merely repricing a product launch; it was rethinking what kind of company Arm had become.

## The Financial Scaffolding

The quarter in which the AGI CPU launched was itself a record. Q4 fiscal 2026, ended March 31, 2026, produced $1.49 billion in revenue — the single largest quarter in Arm's history — and capped a fiscal year in which the company reported total revenue of $4.92 billion, a roughly 24 percent increase over fiscal 2025's approximately $4.0 billion. That figure comprises two streams: royalty revenue of $2.61 billion, up 21 percent year-over-year, and license and other revenue of $2.31 billion, up 25 percent. Non-GAAP earnings per share reached a record $1.77. The balance sheet carried no material long-term debt and more than $3 billion in cash and short-term investments at fiscal year-end, a reflection of the capital-light economics that have defined the IP licensing model since Arm's founding as a joint venture between Acorn Computers, Apple, and VLSI Technology in 1990.

Within the royalty line, the most consequential development was structural rather than volumetric. Data center royalty revenue more than doubled year-over-year in Q4 fiscal 2026, driven by hyperscaler deployments of custom Arm-based silicon — Amazon's Graviton, Google's Axion, and Microsoft's Cobalt 100 — each running on Armv9 cores and each paying royalty rates that are approximately double those commanded by the Armv8 generation they are displacing. AWS reported that the majority of compute capacity added to its fleet in calendar 2025 was Graviton-powered, with its custom silicon business running at more than $20 billion annually.

## Three Compounding Pillars

The investment thesis for Arm rests on three structural forces that are simultaneously expanding the royalty pool, lifting the average royalty rate per chip, and opening an entirely new revenue vertical in physical silicon.

The first and most immediate is the Armv9 mix-shift. Armv9, released in 2021, mandates Scalable Vector Extension 2 for AI inference workloads and Confidential Compute Architecture for hardware-level security isolation — capabilities that justify approximately double the per-chip royalty of the incumbent Armv8 standard. As of Q4 fiscal 2025, Armv9 crossed 30 percent of total royalty income for the first time, and every major smartphone SoC roadmap was already committed to v9 through fiscal 2026 and beyond. This means the blended royalty yield across the installed base compounds upward through mix-shift alone, without requiring a single incremental design win.

The second pillar is Compute Subsystems. Rather than licensing individual CPU cores, Arm now delivers fully integrated, pre-validated subsystem blueprints — CPU cluster, memory subsystem, interconnect, and security IP — that a customer can carry directly to a foundry. CSS royalty rates are approximately double those of standalone core licenses, reflecting the substantially higher engineering value absorbed by the customer. By April 2026, Arm had signed 21 CSS licenses across 12 companies, with five already shipping CSS-based products, including Samsung's Exynos processors.

The third pillar — longer-dated and more uncertain — is the AGI CPU and the physical silicon option it represents. For three decades, Arm's economics were bounded by the royalty fraction it could extract from chips built by others. The AGI CPU changes that boundary, positioning Arm to compete for product-level economics in the data center alongside, and occasionally against, its own licensees.

## The Haas Signature and the Road to $25 Billion

Haas, who became chief executive in February 2022 after running Arm's IP division since 2017, has consistently described Arm's strategy as capturing more of the value it creates rather than simply creating more of it. His tenure has been defined less by architectural invention — the engineering continuity predates him — than by a systematic repricing of Arm's position across the semiconductor stack.

On March 30, 2026, six days after the AGI CPU launch, Arm and SoftBank Group jointly published a roadmap titled "Building a $25 Billion Revenue Business," projecting a roughly fivefold expansion from the fiscal 2026 base. At approximately $222 billion in market capitalization as of May 2026, trading at roughly 45 times fiscal 2026 revenue, the market was already pricing in substantial execution on that path. The dossier that follows examines whether the building blocks — the Armv9 royalty inflection, the CSS adoption curve, the hyperscaler infrastructure bet, and the audacious step into physical silicon — are credible enough to justify the distance between $4.92 billion and the aspiration that lies five times beyond it.

chapters.title: Thirty-Six Years of Quiet Dominance: From the Acorn-Apple Joint Venture to Nasdaq and the AGI CPU
chapters.body:
## Three Companies, One Problem

In the autumn of 1990, three organisations found themselves sharing a single inconvenient fact: none of them could build the processor they needed alone. Acorn Computers, the Cambridge-based maker of the BBC Micro, had been developing an in-house RISC chip since 1983 — the ARM, or Acorn RISC Machine — but lacked the capital and sales reach to commercialise it beyond its own narrow product line. Apple Computer needed a low-power, high-performance processor to animate its Newton personal digital assistant, a device that represented Steve Jobs's successor John Sculley's boldest product bet. VLSI Technology, a Silicon Valley chip fabricator, wanted a foothold in what it believed would become the dominant processor architecture for battery-powered devices. The joint venture they created — incorporated on November 12, 1990, as Widelogic Limited, renamed Advanced RISC Machines Limited three weeks later — was less a strategic masterstroke than an arranged marriage of complementary desperation.

The engineering premise was clean even if the commercial path was not. RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computing) prioritised small, power-efficient instructions over the complex instruction sets Intel had built its franchise upon. For a handheld device that would run on AA batteries, the choice was obvious. Apple provided funding and the Newton design brief; Acorn contributed its engineers and the existing ARM architecture; VLSI contributed fabrication capacity and manufacturing credibility. The combined entity set up offices in a converted barn in Swaffham Bulbeck, outside Cambridge, with twelve engineers transferred from Acorn. It was not, by any conventional measure, a grand founding.

The Newton launched in 1993 and disappointed commercially. The ARM chip inside it, however, did not. By the mid-1990s Nokia had designed the ARM architecture into its GSM handsets — most consequentially the Nokia 6110, which shipped in 1997 carrying what became known as Armv4, an instruction set whose low power draw and compact die footprint made it nearly ideal for mobile phones that needed to last days between charges. This single design win would reshape the trajectory of the company more than any other in its first decade.

## The IPO and the Nokia Effect

Arm floated simultaneously on the London Stock Exchange and Nasdaq on April 17, 1998, raising roughly $175 million and valuing the company at approximately $800 million. The timing proved fortunate. The mobile phone market was beginning an expansion curve that would ultimately prove to be among the fastest in consumer technology history. Nokia alone would ship hundreds of millions of handsets over the following decade, nearly all of them running ARM-based chips. Texas Instruments, which supplied baseband and application processors to Nokia, became one of the most significant ARM licensees of the era. By the early 2000s, ARM's licensing model — charge once for the right to design, collect a royalty on every chip shipped — had demonstrated a compelling flywheel: as more handset makers adopted the architecture, more chip companies sought ARM licences, which funded more architectural development, which attracted more handset makers.

The technology milestones tracked the business inflection points almost exactly. Armv7, introduced in 2004, provided the architectural foundation for the smartphone era that Apple's iPhone inaugurated in 2007. The original iPhone's Samsung-fabbed application processor carried ARM Cortex-A8 cores running Armv7 instructions. When Apple later introduced the A4 chip in 2010, designed entirely in-house but built on Arm licences, it signalled the beginning of the custom-core era that would eventually reshape the entire semiconductor industry. By the time Apple transitioned its Mac computers to its own M-series silicon in 2020, every chip in the world's most valuable consumer electronics portfolio traced its instruction set lineage to that Cambridge barn.

The Armv8 architecture, launched in 2011, introduced 64-bit computing to mobile for the first time. Apple's A7 chip in the iPhone 5s, released in 2013, became the first consumer device to ship a 64-bit ARM processor — catching Qualcomm and Samsung flat-footed and accelerating the industry-wide migration to 64-bit that Arm had anticipated. Armv8 would remain the dominant shipping architecture for most of the following decade, establishing the royalty baseline against which Armv9's economics would later be measured.

## SoftBank and the Singularity Thesis

By July 2016, Arm had become the default architecture for mobile computing globally, with its technology shipping in roughly 95 percent of the world's smartphones. That dominance attracted Masayoshi Son, SoftBank's founder and chief executive, who announced an agreed all-cash acquisition of Arm for £23.4 billion — approximately $32 billion at prevailing exchange rates — on July 18, 2016. The deal, completed September 5, 2016, was the largest acquisition of a European technology company ever recorded at that point.

Son's public rationale went considerably beyond mobile. He spoke of the Internet of Things, of one trillion connected devices requiring processors within a decade, and of what he called "the singularity" — a moment at which artificial intelligence would surpass human intelligence and demand ubiquitous, low-power computation. Whether or not one accepted the eschatology, the operational logic was straightforward: whoever licensed the dominant CPU architecture would collect a royalty on every chip inside every connected device. SoftBank, which had spent the prior decade assembling telecommunications assets, was making a different kind of bet — on the architecture layer rather than the network layer.

In 2017, SoftBank transferred a 25 percent stake in Arm to its newly formed SoftBank Vision Fund, the $100 billion technology investment vehicle backed by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund and Abu Dhabi's Mubadala. The Vision Fund stake would later complicate Arm's path back to public markets.

## The Nvidia Attempt and Its Collapse

In September 2020, Nvidia announced an agreement to acquire Arm from SoftBank for $40 billion — $21.5 billion in Nvidia stock, $12 billion in cash and stock at closing, and a further $5 billion contingent earnout. The strategic logic, from Nvidia's perspective, was the combination of Arm's ubiquitous CPU architecture with Nvidia's dominant GPU franchise, creating a potential platform spanning mobile, edge, and data centre compute.

Regulators saw it differently. The United States Federal Trade Commission filed suit in December 2021, arguing the deal would give Nvidia the ability and incentive to disadvantage rival chip designers who depended on Arm's IP. The United Kingdom's Competition and Markets Authority launched its own Phase 2 investigation. The European Commission opened a formal probe. Chinese regulators, whose approval was required given Arm's substantial business in China, showed no sign of clearing the transaction.

By February 2022, with all four major regulatory proceedings unresolved and Nvidia's stock price having fallen materially from the announcement levels — reducing the effective value of the stock consideration — the parties abandoned the deal. The formal termination came on February 8, 2022. Three days earlier, Simon Segars, who had served as Arm's chief executive since 2013, stepped down. His successor, announced simultaneously, was Rene Haas, who had run Arm's IP division since 2017 and, before that, had spent seven years at Nvidia as vice president and general manager of its computing products group — making him, by a certain irony, a product of both institutions whose union had just failed.

## The IPO and the Ownership Paradox

With the Nvidia path closed, SoftBank moved to return Arm to public markets. In August 2023, SoftBank reacquired Vision Fund's 25 percent stake for approximately $16.1 billion, consolidating 100 percent ownership ahead of an offering. On September 14, 2023, Arm listed on Nasdaq under the ticker ARM, raising $5.23 billion in the largest technology IPO of that year. The offering priced shares at $51, valuing the company at approximately $54.5 billion. Demand was sufficient that the order book reportedly closed within an hour of opening.

| Event | Date | Valuation / Proceeds |
|---|---|---|
| LSE / Nasdaq dual listing | April 1998 | ~$800 million |
| SoftBank acquisition | September 2016 | £23.4 billion (~$32 billion) |
| Vision Fund stake reacquired | August 2023 | ~$16.1 billion (25% stake) |
| Nasdaq IPO | September 2023 | $5.23 billion raised; ~$54.5 billion valuation |

The ownership structure that emerged from the IPO contained an inherent paradox. SoftBank retained approximately 89.9 percent of Arm's outstanding shares following the offering, leaving a public float so thin that Arm's share price would prove highly sensitive to sentiment shifts and index inclusion events. In March 2024, Arm was added to the Nasdaq-100, driving passive fund buying that pushed the stock above $160 — a market capitalisation exceeding $165 billion — before it retreated. The company was simultaneously a public company subject to SEC disclosure requirements and quarterly earnings scrutiny, and a controlled subsidiary whose strategic direction remained subject to the capital allocation priorities of a single Japanese conglomerate.

That structural tension has defined Arm's public-company chapter. In fiscal year 2026, ended March 31, 2026, Arm reported record revenue of $4.92 billion — more than double its fiscal 2022 revenue — with Armv9 chips crossing 30 percent of total royalty income and data centre royalties more than doubling year-over-year. On March 24, 2026, the company announced the AGI CPU, its first internally designed physical silicon product in thirty-five years of existence, targeting the agentic AI workload market with committed demand exceeding $2 billion. Six days later, Arm and SoftBank presented a joint roadmap projecting $25 billion in annual revenue — a roughly fivefold expansion from the IPO-year base.

The company that Acorn, Apple, and VLSI Technology assembled in a converted barn to solve a battery problem had, across thirty-six years, become the instruction set substrate for the world's computing infrastructure. The next inflection — from IP licensor to silicon manufacturer, from royalty collector to product company — was the most structurally consequential since the Nokia 6110 first shipped with an ARM core in its baseband.

chapters.title: The IP Stack: Cortex Families, Neoverse, Compute Subsystems, and the First-Silicon Leap with the AGI CPU
chapters.body:
## The Foundation: Cortex-M and Cortex-R in the Embedded World

Arm's product stack begins not in the hyperscale data center but in the microcontroller — the invisible processor embedded in thermostats, brake sensors, industrial pumps, and hearing aids. The Cortex-M series, introduced in 2004, became the default compute fabric of the physical world. STMicroelectronics alone had shipped billions of STM32 Cortex-M units by the mid-2020s; Infineon, Nordic Semiconductor, and Texas Instruments built major businesses on the same architecture. Royalty rates per Cortex-M core are modest — these are $1–$3 chips in commodity volumes — but the aggregate royalty contribution from tens of billions of annual shipments provides Arm with a durable base-load revenue floor that is structurally independent of any single end market.

The Cortex-R family occupies the tier above: real-time processors for applications where deterministic latency is a regulatory or safety requirement. Automotive electronic control units, storage device controllers, and 5G baseband modems depend on Cortex-R for their hard real-time guarantees. NXP Semiconductors' S32 automotive platform, Renesas's R-Car family, and Mobileye's driver assistance processors all draw on Cortex-R lineage. Though lower in headline profile than the Cortex-A or Neoverse families, the Cortex-R embedded in automotive systems carries higher average selling prices than consumer IoT, and the industry's transition to software-defined vehicles is steadily adding more R-series cores per car.

## Cortex-A and the Mobile Engine Room

The Cortex-A series built the modern smartphone. From the first Cortex-A8 to the current Cortex-X Elite, this family has provided the performance-per-watt envelope that enabled Apple's iPhone, Qualcomm's Snapdragon, and Samsung's Exynos to outrun Intel's mobile ambitions and entrench Arm as the dominant architecture for portable compute. Arm does not disclose per-licensee revenue, but the concentration is evident: Apple's A-series and M-series custom cores, Qualcomm's Oryon, MediaTek's Dimensity, and Samsung's Exynos collectively represent the majority of smartphone processors shipped globally, and all are Armv9-based as of fiscal 2026.

The Armv9 architecture — released in 2021 and entering volume production across the SoC roadmaps of every major smartphone OEM by fiscal 2025 — is the most consequential royalty rate inflection in Arm's thirty-five-year history. The architecture's mandatory inclusion of the Scalable Vector Extension 2 (SVE2) provides hardware-native support for the matrix and vector operations at the core of on-device AI inference, enabling features from real-time photo enhancement to local large-language-model inference without cloud round-trips. The Confidential Compute Architecture (CCA) establishes hardware-enforced security realms that isolate sensitive workloads from the operating system and hypervisor, addressing the regulatory requirements increasingly imposed on mobile payment, health, and enterprise applications. Memory tagging extensions add hardware-level detection of buffer overflows and use-after-free vulnerabilities, hardening the security posture at the silicon level.

Together, these capabilities justify Arm's position that Armv9 commands approximately double the royalty rate per chip of its Armv8 predecessor. The royalty uplift accrues not through renegotiation of existing contracts but through mix-shift: as licensees retire their Armv8 designs and move volume to Armv9, the blended royalty yield per chip shipped rises structurally. By Q4 fiscal 2025 — the quarter ended March 31, 2025 — Armv9 had crossed 30 percent of total royalty income for the first time, confirming that the inflection was translating from design-win momentum into cash royalties.

## Neoverse and the Data Center Conversion

The Neoverse platform, launched in 2018, was Arm's declaration that it intended to compete for data center compute, not merely supply it at the margins. The architecture's trajectory vindicated that ambition. Amazon's Graviton processors — now powering the majority of compute capacity the company added to its AWS fleet in 2025, with the AWS custom silicon business running at more than $20 billion annually — are Neoverse-based. Google's Axion processor, deployed to migrate more than 30,000 cloud applications to Arm infrastructure, uses Neoverse. Microsoft's Cobalt 100, deployed across 29 global Azure regions, and Nvidia's Grace and Vera processors for AI infrastructure are both built on Neoverse IP. The cumulative effect compressed Arm's data center royalty revenue trajectory: data center royalties more than doubled year-over-year in Q4 fiscal 2026.

The data center matters to Arm's royalty economics in a way that mobile cannot fully replicate. A server CPU carries an average selling price an order of magnitude above a smartphone application processor; the royalty, calculated as a percentage of that ASP, scales accordingly. Arm's server CPU market share was projected to expand from 13.4 percent in 2025 to 23.1 percent in 2028, and each percentage point of share gained at data center ASPs delivers royalty yield that would require hundreds of millions of mobile chip shipments to replicate.

Mali GPU IP and the AMBA interconnect portfolio — CoreLink cache coherency fabric, AHB and AXI bus protocols — sit alongside Neoverse as lower-profile but volume-essential product lines. Mali GPU cores ship in hundreds of millions of mid-range Android handsets and embedded displays annually. AMBA interconnect, included in virtually every Arm-based SoC regardless of the CPU family, generates royalties that are durable and largely invisible in competitive analysis precisely because they are so embedded in standard design practice.

## Compute Subsystems: Selling the Blueprint, Not Just the Brick

Arm Compute Subsystems represent the most sophisticated tier of the company's IP portfolio below physical silicon. Rather than licensing a standalone CPU core that a chip designer must then integrate with memory subsystems, interconnect fabric, security processors, and I/O controllers — a process requiring months of engineering validation — CSS delivers a pre-integrated, foundry-validated blueprint encompassing the CPU cluster, the memory subsystem, the AMBA interconnect, and the security IP as a single tested unit. The licensee receives something close to a proven chiplet design ready to submit for tape-out.

The commercial logic is straightforward. The engineering value delivered by CSS — reduced time-to-market, lower integration risk, validated power and performance targets — supports a royalty rate approximately double that of a standalone core license. By April 2026, Arm had signed 21 CSS licenses across 12 companies, up from 19 licenses at the time of the Q2 fiscal 2026 earnings call, and five customers were already shipping CSS-powered products in volume. Samsung's Exynos mobile processors were among the first CSS-integrated chips to reach consumers, and Arm noted that its top four Android phone vendors were collectively CSS-powered by that point. The scaling from concept to 21 licenses in a product category that did not exist before 2019 validated CSS as a structural royalty rate lever rather than a niche offering.

## The AGI CPU: First Silicon, Maximum Tension

On March 24, 2026, Arm crossed a boundary it had never crossed in 35 years of operation: it announced a physical chip. The Arm AGI CPU is a 3-nanometer data center processor built on the Neoverse V3 architecture, targeted at agentic AI inference workloads. The reference 1OU dual-node blade packs 272 Arm cores; scaled to a full rack in a 36kW air-cooled configuration, the system delivers 8,160 cores. Arm claimed 2x performance-per-rack versus comparable x86 configurations, a figure the company attributed to the architectural efficiency of Armv9 combined with optimized memory bandwidth and interconnect topology for transformer-class models. Meta served as the lead development partner throughout the design process, and launch partners at announcement included OpenAI, Cloudflare, Cerebras, SAP, and SK Telecom, with system integrators Lenovo, Supermicro, and ASRockRack offering production systems to order. Committed customer demand for the AGI CPU exceeded $2 billion across fiscal years 2027 and 2028.

The product's strategic implications extend well beyond the addressable market for one chip. The AGI CPU is simultaneously Arm's highest-royalty product — because Arm captures product-level margin on its own silicon rather than a per-chip royalty fraction — and its most structurally ambiguous. For three and a half decades, Arm's competitive position rested on a foundational promise to licensees: the company would never compete with them in the product market. Qualcomm, MediaTek, Apple, and dozens of other chip designers paid licensing fees and royalties in the secure knowledge that Arm would supply them all neutrally.

The AGI CPU complicates that promise at the margin. Management addressed the tension in launch communications by framing the AGI CPU as a new category — an Arm-branded system optimized for a workload class that Arm's licensees were not, in the company's characterization, adequately serving — rather than a direct alternative to Qualcomm's server roadmap or Apple's custom silicon. The distinction is defensible for now: the AGI CPU targets cloud-scale agentic AI inference, a market segment that Qualcomm and MediaTek do not presently address at data center scale, and Apple does not license its custom cores externally. But the competitive logic that justifies the AGI CPU today — that Arm can serve end markets its licensees leave unaddressed — is expandable, and licensees will monitor future product announcements accordingly.

The $25 billion revenue roadmap presented jointly by Arm and SoftBank on March 30, 2026 provides the frame within which management has asked investors to read the silicon pivot. A roughly 5x expansion from the fiscal 2026 base of $4.92 billion implies that the AGI CPU silicon business, alongside Armv9 royalty mix-shift and CSS volume scale, must each contribute materially. At the margin, the AGI CPU is not a threat to the licensing business that built Arm; it is the licensing business's argument that per-chip royalty economics, however structurally improving, are insufficient to capture the value Arm's architecture generates at the system level.

chapters.title: The Royalty Machine: Revenue Trajectory, Margin Architecture, and the Capital Structure of an IP Monopoly
chapters.body:
## Two Streams, One Machine

Arm Holdings does not make chips. It makes the right to make chips — and then collects a toll on every one that ships. The elegance of that business model, and the financial architecture it produces, is best understood by decomposing it into the two revenue streams that have driven the company to its current scale: royalties, which are the per-chip economics embedded in thirty billion devices shipped annually, and licensing fees, which are the upfront payments that create tomorrow's royalty contributors today.

In fiscal year 2026, ending March 31, 2026, those two streams combined to produce $4.92 billion in total revenue — a record for the company and approximately 24 percent above the $4.0 billion posted in fiscal 2025, which itself had grown 21 percent over the prior year. The acceleration was not accidental. It reflected the compounding effect of two structural tailwinds arriving simultaneously: the royalty rate inflation embedded in the Armv9 architecture transition, and a licensing pipeline filling with hyperscaler custom silicon programs that would take years to begin generating royalties but were already triggering substantial recognition milestones.

## Quarterly Cadence: The Acceleration Years

The quarterly progression through fiscal years 2025 and 2026 illustrated how those two forces moved on different timescales. Licensing revenue, which is recognized when contractual milestones are reached rather than when chips ship, tends to move in lumps determined by the timing of contract completions and deliverable sign-offs. Royalty revenue, by contrast, follows the cadence of the global semiconductor supply chain — recognized when chips leave the foundry, smoothed across inventory cycles, and highly recurring in aggregate even as individual customers fluctuate.

Across fiscal 2025, total revenue of approximately $4.0 billion reflected a period in which Armv9 penetration was still relatively early — the architecture crossed 30 percent of royalty income only in Q4 fiscal 2025 — while licensing revenue was buoyed by the broadening of the Compute Subsystems (CSS) program and ongoing Neoverse data center engagements. The royalty and licensing streams ran roughly in balance through fiscal 2025.

The growth rate stepped up meaningfully in fiscal 2026. By the second quarter of the year — the three months ended September 30, 2025 — total revenue had grown 34 percent year-over-year, marking one of the company's strongest quarterly growth rates since its Nasdaq listing in September 2023. The second half of fiscal 2026 saw further momentum, with Q4 fiscal 2026 becoming the single largest quarter in company history at $1.49 billion.

| Quarter | Total Revenue | Licensing | Royalty | YoY Growth (Total) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q4 FY2026 | $1.49B | $819M | $671M | — |
| Q4 FY2026 YoY | — | +29% | +11% | — |
| Q2 FY2026 | — | — | — | +34% |
| FY2026 Full Year | $4.92B | $2.31B | $2.61B | ~+24% |
| FY2025 Full Year | ~$4.0B | ~$1.85B | ~$2.16B | ~+21% |

Within Q4 fiscal 2026, the divergence between the two streams was telling. Licensing grew 29 percent year-over-year while royalties grew 11 percent — reflecting the lag between when programs are contracted and when chips begin shipping in volume. The $819 million in quarterly licensing revenue was a record high, consistent with a robust pipeline of new CSS agreements and hyperscaler contracts completing milestone phases. The 11 percent royalty growth for the same quarter, against a backdrop of global smartphone unit growth measured in low single digits, confirmed that the per-chip yield expansion from Armv9 mix-shift was providing a meaningful uplift above unit volume alone.

## The Royalty Flywheel vs. the Licensing Pulse

Understanding the difference in recognition mechanics matters because it shapes how investors should read any given quarter. Royalty revenue is recognized on a one-quarter lag — Arm collects reports from licensees and recognizes revenue in the quarter after chips ship, smoothing what would otherwise be a volatile demand signal into a relatively steady stream. The stickiness of the royalty base is structural: once an architecture is designed into a chip, it ships in that chip for years. A smartphone SoC designed on Armv9 in 2024 will generate Armv9 royalties every time it appears in a handset through the late 2020s.

Licensing revenue is the inverse: it is lumpy by design, because it reflects the contractual lifecycle of technology agreements that can range from relatively modest IoT licenses to the multi-hundred-million-dollar total contracts associated with hyperscaler custom silicon programs. A quarter in which several large programs complete milestones simultaneously will show a license revenue spike; the subsequent quarters may be quieter until the next tranche of programs reaches completion. This makes licensing a reliable leading indicator of future royalty contributors — every signed CSS agreement or architectural license eventually becomes a royalty stream — but a poor guide to near-term smoothed earnings.

The Compute Subsystems product sharpens this dynamic. By April 2026, Arm had signed 21 CSS licenses across 12 companies, with five customers already shipping CSS-based chips including Samsung's Exynos mobile processors. CSS royalty rates run approximately double those of standalone core licenses, reflecting the greater engineering value delivered in a pre-integrated subsystem. When those CSS chips begin shipping in volume — and the top four Android smartphone vendors were already committed to CSS integration — they will lift the blended royalty yield per unit shipped relative to the legacy mix.

## Margin Architecture: The SBC Problem and the Non-GAAP Answer

The raw financial statements of Arm Holdings look, at first inspection, like those of a company generating significantly less profit than its revenue scale would suggest. That appearance is misleading, and the reason is stock-based compensation.

Arm carries a substantial SBC burden, a legacy of pre-IPO equity grants calibrated when the company was private and employee compensation was delivered primarily through equity, combined with ongoing incentive programs for a global engineering workforce competing with the highest-paying employers in the semiconductor industry. These charges, which flow through the income statement as operating expense, compress GAAP operating margins to a fraction of the true economic earnings power of the IP licensing model.

The royalty business, stripped of SBC allocation, carries gross margins in the mid-to-high nineties — the cost of earning royalty revenue is essentially zero once the underlying architecture has been developed and licensed. Licensing revenue carries somewhat lower gross margins given the cost of engineering delivery against milestones, but the blended gross margin of the IP licensing business remains structurally very high. For fiscal 2026, non-GAAP earnings per share reached a record $1.77 on $4.92 billion in revenue, implying a non-GAAP operating margin in the high thirties to mid-forties percentage range. The gap between GAAP and non-GAAP reflects SBC that, in fiscal years 2025 and 2026, consumed a material fraction of total revenue — consistent with the disclosures in Arm's 20-F annual filings, which detailed SBC as a significant line item running well into the hundreds of millions of dollars annually.

The market has, from the outset, priced Arm on non-GAAP metrics. At a market capitalization of approximately $222 billion and an enterprise value of approximately $219 billion as of early May 2026, the implied non-GAAP price-to-earnings multiple ran to approximately 115 times fiscal 2026 non-GAAP earnings — a valuation that embeds not merely current profitability but a full scenario of Armv9 royalty yield expansion, CSS volume ramp, and the revenue optionality of the nascent AGI CPU silicon business.

## The Balance Sheet: Cash-Rich, Debt-Free

The IP licensing model generates cash with a simplicity that capital-intensive businesses can rarely match. Arm does not build fabs. It does not carry inventory. Its principal assets are the engineering talent and accumulated design work that produce the IP, and it pays for those primarily in the very compensation that creates the SBC charges that compress its GAAP earnings.

As of March 31, 2026, cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments on the balance sheet exceeded $3 billion. Long-term debt was not a material feature of the capital structure — a direct reflection of the model's ability to fund its operations from internally generated cash without recourse to leverage. Free cash flow conversion, while not disclosed at a precise figure in the prep materials, is structurally strong: the business has minimal capital expenditure requirements in its traditional IP licensing form, and even the substantial ongoing R&D investment required to maintain architectural leadership does not require the fixed-asset spending that would drag on a semiconductor manufacturer.

The strategic shift into physical silicon through the AGI CPU will change this calculus modestly but materially. Designing, validating, and bringing to production a 3nm data center chip requires non-recurring engineering arrangements with foundry partners, testing infrastructure, and supply chain relationships that a pure IP licensor has historically not needed. The more than $2 billion in committed customer demand for the AGI CPU across fiscal years 2027 and 2028 suggests the revenue opportunity is real, but the investment required to deliver it will be the first significant drawdown on the IP licensing model's historically frictionless cash generation.

## China: The 25 Percent Risk Premium

Geographic revenue concentration represents the most structurally embedded risk in Arm's financial model. China has historically accounted for approximately 25 percent of total revenue, a figure that reflects the density of Chinese chip designers — from smartphone SoC makers like MediaTek's Chinese licensees and HiSilicon through to a broad tail of IoT and industrial chip companies — that have built their products on Arm architectures.

The China royalty stream is vulnerable to two distinct disruption mechanisms. The first is geopolitical: tightening export controls on advanced chip technology could, depending on their precise scope, restrict Arm's ability to license certain architectural generations to Chinese companies, or could trigger retaliatory restrictions from Beijing on Chinese companies' use of foreign IP. The second is competitive: RISC-V, the open-source instruction set architecture that requires no licensing fees, has found its strongest adoption precisely in China, where the strategic motivation to reduce dependence on Western IP is most acute. By late 2025, RISC-V claimed roughly 25 percent market penetration across relevant semiconductor segments globally, with concentration notably higher in China's IoT and industrial embedded markets.

Any sustained disruption to the China royalty stream — whether through licensing restrictions, customer migration to RISC-V, or a deterioration in the Armv9 upgrade cycle among Chinese handset chip designers — would remove approximately one-quarter of the current revenue base and disproportionately affect the recurring, highly-margin royalty stream rather than the relatively more diversified licensing pipeline.

## The Road to $25 Billion

Arm guided the first quarter of fiscal 2027 to $1.26 billion, plus or minus $50 million. Against the fiscal 2026 full-year base of $4.92 billion, that guidance midpoint represents an annualized run-rate of slightly over $5 billion — consistent with the analyst consensus of approximately $5.99 billion for the full fiscal 2027 year, implying approximately 20 percent year-over-year growth continuing the deceleration from the 34 percent peak posted in Q2 fiscal 2026.

The $25 billion long-range roadmap, jointly presented by Arm and SoftBank Group in March 2026, implies a roughly five-times expansion of the fiscal 2026 revenue base. The arithmetic of that target requires each of the company's growth engines to perform simultaneously and at scale. Armv9 royalty mix-shift, continuing to push the blended per-chip royalty rate toward the theoretical ceiling represented by a fully-transitioned installed base, could add several hundred million dollars annually over the next three to four years. CSS adoption across the top Android smartphone vendors, expanding to the automotive and infrastructure segments where Arm has signed but not yet broadly shipped, would compound that further. Data center royalties — which more than doubled year-over-year in Q4 fiscal 2026 — represent the fastest-growing segment but remain below the mobile royalty base in absolute scale.

The AGI CPU is the variable that makes $25 billion plausible rather than merely aspirational. At $15 billion in projected peak annual revenue for that product line alone — more than three times Arm's entire fiscal 2026 revenue — it is not a royalty rate optimization but a category creation: Arm becoming, for the first time in its 35-year history, a company that competes for product-level economics in the most valuable part of the global compute stack. Whether the financial model can deliver that outcome will depend on execution against a silicon product roadmap for which Arm has no institutional precedent, in a data center market where hyperscalers have already demonstrated they will build their own custom designs if a supplier cannot meet their price or performance requirements. The royalty machine runs reliably. The silicon business is, as yet, unproven — and the path from $4.92 billion to $25 billion runs straight through it.

chapters.title: Pricing the Architecture: Multiples, Intrinsic Value, and the Market's Embedded AI Premium
chapters.body:
## The Weight of Expectation

At the close of trading on May 23, 2026, Arm Holdings carried a market capitalization of approximately $222 billion and an enterprise value of approximately $219 billion — a figure that, set against fiscal 2026 revenue of $4.92 billion, produced a trailing EV/revenue multiple of roughly 44.5x. The forward multiple on consensus fiscal 2027 revenue of approximately $5.99 billion settled near 37x. The non-GAAP trailing price-to-earnings ratio stood near 115x; strip out the stock-based compensation charges that make non-GAAP the operative metric across semiconductor IP, and the GAAP trailing P/E reached approximately 357x.

These are not numbers that emerge from conventional discounted cash flow analysis or standard peer comparison exercises. They are the arithmetic expression of a market consensus that Arm is a different kind of company than the one that floated on Nasdaq at $51 per share in September 2023 — one that has, over thirty-two months as a public company, converted a profitable licensing business into what many investors now treat as a pure-play AI infrastructure platform with the royalty economics of a tollbooth and the silicon ambitions of a startup.

## Peer Context: A Premium Without a Ceiling

The standard framework for valuing semiconductor IP licensors reaches for ASML, Synopsys, and Cadence as the nearest structural analogues — businesses with similarly high gross margins, recurring revenue characteristics, and technology moats that competitors cannot replicate in a product cycle. Arm trades at a material premium to each of them, and to the leading fabless and platform semiconductor companies besides.

| Company | Business | Trailing EV/Rev | Forward EV/Rev | Forward P/E | EV/EBITDA | ARM Fwd-Rev Premium |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Arm Holdings** | CPU IP / silicon | 44.5x | 36.6x | ~92x (non-GAAP fwd) | ~90x | — |
| ASML | Semiconductor equipment IP | ~9x | ~8x | ~27x | ~21x | **+29x** |
| Synopsys | EDA + IP | ~11x | ~10x | ~32x | ~26x | **+27x** |
| Cadence | EDA + IP | ~13x | ~11x | ~34x | ~28x | **+26x** |
| Qualcomm | Fabless (mobile/PC) | ~3.5x | ~3.2x | ~13x | ~9x | **+33x** |
| Broadcom | Diversified semiconductor | ~13x | ~11x | ~22x | ~16x | **+26x** |
| NVIDIA | GPU platform | ~16x | ~14x | ~30x | ~24x | **+23x** |

*Approximate as of May 23, 2026. Arm forward P/E on non-GAAP consensus FY2027 EPS; trailing non-GAAP P/E is approximately 115x.*

The comparison with NVIDIA was the most analytically revealing. NVIDIA commanded the richest multiple in the broader semiconductor universe on the basis of GPU platform dominance in AI infrastructure, yet Arm still traded at more than twice NVIDIA's forward EV/revenue ratio. The implicit argument was that Arm's royalty model — structurally asset-light, with no manufacturing exposure and a rate structure that compounds arithmetically with every architecture generation — deserved a premium over even the most successful fabless chip company. The gap was also a function of scale: NVIDIA's revenue base had grown large enough to make a 14–16x EV/revenue multiple arithmetic, while Arm's $4.92 billion fiscal 2026 revenue left enormous room for the numerator to expand before the multiple compressed. At the other extreme, Qualcomm's sub-4x EV/revenue reflected both maturation risk in the Android handset market and the absence of any compounding royalty-rate mechanism — exactly the structural quality Arm had spent three years demonstrating it possessed.

## A Stock That Re-Rated Three Times in Thirty Months

The September 2023 IPO priced at $51 per share, valuing Arm at approximately $54.5 billion. Against trailing fiscal 2023 revenue of approximately $2.68 billion, the IPO implied a trailing EV/revenue of approximately 19x — elevated relative to pure semiconductor companies but within reach of software-comparable multiples for an IP licensor. The forward EV/NTM revenue at IPO was approximately 14–16x.

The stock re-rated sharply in early 2024 as the AI investment cycle broadened from GPU infrastructure to CPU efficiency. EV/NTM revenue peaked near 50x in February 2024 before a correction pulled the multiple back toward 15–20x in the second half of 2024, when growth-at-any-price enthusiasm cooled and analysts questioned whether Arm's royalty beats reflected structural rate improvement or one-time licensing catch-up payments. The re-rating resumed through fiscal 2025 earnings beats, each quarter confirming that Armv9 mix-shift was compounding royalty yield independent of unit volume. By the time the AGI CPU launched on March 24, 2026 — with committed customer demand exceeding $2 billion and Meta as lead development partner — the stock had already recovered to the mid-to-high 30x EV/NTM range. The six weeks that followed added approximately 71 percent to the share price, pushing EV/NTM briefly above 45x before settling near 37x at the frozen snapshot.

The full historical range since IPO: approximately **14x** EV/NTM revenue at the 2024 trough to approximately **50x** at the early-2024 and post-AGI CPU announcement peaks. The stock entered the frozen window near the upper quartile of its own history, having traversed four distinct sentiment regimes in under three years.

## Three Scenarios

The following scenarios are indexed to fiscal 2027 revenue and the forward EV/revenue multiple the market sustains. Arm's share count is approximately 1.05 billion; net cash is approximately $3 billion.

**Bull — Armv9 Accelerates, CSS Scales, AGI CPU Lands on Schedule.** Armv9 royalty mix reaches 60 percent of royalty revenue by fiscal 2028, well ahead of consensus; CSS licenses grow from 21 to 40 entities within 24 months; the AGI CPU delivers $1.5 billion in fiscal 2027 revenue as Meta and OpenAI deployments ramp faster than guided. Fiscal 2027 revenue reaches approximately $7.5 billion. The market sustains a 40x forward EV/revenue multiple on the argument that the AGI CPU business warrants a product-company premium layered onto the IP-licensor floor. **Implied EV approximately $300 billion; market capitalization approximately $303 billion; per-share value approximately $289.**

**Base — Consensus Path, CSS on Track, AGI CPU Contributes Moderately.** Armv9 and CSS adoption tracks sell-side consensus. The AGI CPU contributes approximately $500 million to fiscal 2027 revenue, consistent with the $2 billion committed-demand figure spread over two years. Fiscal 2027 revenue reaches approximately $5.99 billion. The market re-rates modestly from current levels to a 30x forward EV/revenue multiple as near-term execution replaces optionality-pricing. **Implied EV approximately $180 billion; market capitalization approximately $183 billion; per-share value approximately $174** — roughly 18 percent below the May 23 price.

**Bear — RISC-V Erosion, AGI CPU Delayed, Multiple Compression.** RISC-V claims accelerating share in Chinese IoT and embedded markets, where Arm historically derived approximately 25 percent of total revenue. Export-control friction compounds domestic architecture substitution pressure. AGI CPU shipments slip to fiscal 2028. Royalty growth decelerates to high single digits. Fiscal 2027 revenue reaches approximately $5.5 billion. The multiple compresses to 20x forward EV/revenue as the tollbooth narrative is stress-tested by volume displacement. **Implied EV approximately $110 billion; market capitalization approximately $113 billion; per-share value approximately $108** — roughly 49 percent below the frozen-window price.

## What the Current Price Embeds

At approximately $211 per share and $219 billion EV, the market was pricing several specific propositions simultaneously. First, approximately 20 percent annual revenue CAGR sustained through fiscal 2030 was necessary but not sufficient — the jointly published $25 billion revenue roadmap implied a compound rate of 26–38 percent from the fiscal 2026 base. Second, the Armv9 royalty yield improvement was real and durable: every percentage point of mix-shift from v8 (where v9 rates are approximately double) flows directly to blended royalty yield without requiring a single new design win, and the market was pricing that compounding through at least fiscal 2028. Third, the AGI CPU reaching $1 billion or more in annual revenue within two to three years was assigned a probability the market treated as meaningfully high — anchored by the $2 billion in committed demand already on the books.

The SoftBank ownership concentration added a structural distortion. With approximately 89.9 percent of shares held by a single parent, the effective public float was thin enough that institutional demand for AI infrastructure exposure had no alternative vehicle in the same risk category. A portion of the multiple premium was, in effect, a scarcity premium.

## DCF Sensitivity

A simplified five-year discounted cash flow, running fiscal 2027 through fiscal 2031, illustrates why the current share price sits above what conventional analysis supports — and what that gap implies. Both scenarios assume approximately 38 percent non-GAAP free cash flow margins and a 30x terminal FCF multiple at fiscal 2031.

| Scenario | FY27E Rev | Rev CAGR to FY31 | FCF FY31 | Term. Value | EV @ 10% DR | EV @ 15% DR | Implied Price @ 10% |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | $7.5B | 24% | $6.8B | $204B | ~$170B | ~$112B | **~$164** |
| Base | $5.99B | 20% | $4.7B | $141B | ~$118B | ~$78B | **~$115** |

*FCF margin 38%; terminal multiple 30x FCF; 1.05B shares; net cash $3B added back. Five-year horizon ends FY2031.*

The result is unambiguous: at a 10 percent discount rate, neither the base nor the bull case in this framework justifies the May 23 price of approximately $211. Closing the gap requires some combination of below-market discount rates — defensible if Arm's royalty stream is treated as infrastructure-like in its predictability — and terminal multiples well above 30x, which only makes sense if the AGI CPU business is eventually valued as a product company rather than a licensing operation. The market was simultaneously discounting at perhaps 7–8 percent and assigning meaningful probability to the AGI CPU's $15 billion annual revenue ambition. That embedded optionality, not the licensing business at current scale, was the variable doing most of the work in the share price. Whether it was warranted would depend on execution — on whether Rene Haas could convert thirty-five years of architectural ubiquity into a product business that the public markets had never asked Arm to build.

chapters.title: Quarter by Quarter: The Armv9 Ramp Told Through Earnings Calls and Financial Print
chapters.body:
## The Hinge Quarter: Q3 FY25 and the Data Center Signal

For most of Arm's post-IPO life as a public company, the stock moved on smartphones: iPhone cycle, Android market share, Qualcomm royalty disputes. The shift in that framing began in the quarter ended December 2024, when Q3 FY25 results demonstrated data center royalties growing at a materially higher rate than mobile, even as the overall royalty line expanded roughly 19 percent year-over-year to approximately $983 million in total revenue. On the February 2025 earnings call, chief executive Rene Haas described the dynamic in terms that would become a recurring framing: "The data center is now our fastest-growing end market, and the customers deploying Arm silicon at scale include every major hyperscaler in the world."

The single metric that defined Q3 FY25 in market perception was not topline revenue but the royalty growth differential: data center royalties were outpacing the blended line by a wide margin, confirming that the shift was structural rather than cyclical. Investors who had priced Arm as a mobile royalty story began repricing it as a data center royalty story, a revaluation that would take several more quarters to fully express itself in the multiples applied to the server market opportunity.

## The 30 Percent Milestone: Q4 FY25

The hinge became a turning point in Q4 FY25, the quarter ended March 2025. Total revenue reached approximately $1.24 billion, beating the high end of guidance by a meaningful margin and setting a new single-quarter record at that time. But the number that moved perception was not the topline—it was the Armv9 royalty mix. On the May 7, 2025 earnings call, Haas delivered the milestone the company had telegraphed for eighteen months:

> "Armv9 royalties exceeded 30 percent of total royalty revenue for the first time in Q4, and every major smartphone and data center roadmap we are aware of is migrating to v9. This matters because Armv9 commands approximately double the royalty rate of Armv8—so every point of mix shift is additive yield, independent of unit volume."

Chief financial officer Jason Child reinforced the structural significance: "We think of the royalty line as having two compounders running simultaneously—Armv9 mix shift and data center share gain. Both are still early. Neither requires the other to be true." The 30 percent threshold represented an inflection, not a ceiling. Move the Armv9 mix from 30 to 60 percent while holding unit volumes flat, and the implied royalty pool nearly doubles on rate alone—a calculus that reshaped how analysts modeled the royalty line's long-term trajectory.

## Building Momentum: Q1 and Q2 FY26

The two quarters spanning April through September 2025—Q1 and Q2 FY26—were quarters of accumulation rather than singular announcements. Revenue expanded from approximately $1.02 billion in Q1 to approximately $1.05 billion in Q2, with each quarter delivering results above the midpoint of guidance. The pattern established in these quarters reflected a management team that had learned to guide conservatively: four consecutive quarters of above-midpoint delivery became an implicit floor for analyst estimates, compressing the risk premium embedded in guidance ranges.

The most important metric in Q1 FY26 was not revenue growth but the Compute Subsystem license count, which continued its methodical rise. By the Q2 FY26 earnings call, Haas disclosed that Arm had signed 19 CSS licenses across 11 companies, with five customers already shipping CSS-based products—Samsung's Exynos processors as the flagship example. The commercial significance was the royalty rate multiplier: CSS licenses carry approximately double the per-chip royalty of standalone core licenses, meaning that a chip shipped under a CSS agreement generates roughly four times the royalty yield of a comparable Armv8 standalone core, compounding both the v9 rate premium and the CSS integration premium.

In Q2 FY26, Haas framed the CSS pipeline in terms of ecosystem capture: "We had five customers already shipping CSS-based products. The first one was Samsung with Exynos, and now every top four Android OEM has CSS at the center of their roadmap."

Revenue recognition accounting introduced comparison complexity throughout fiscal 2026. Large multi-year technology licensing agreements—particularly CSS packages sold to hyperscalers and custom silicon developers—are recognized at contract execution rather than rateably over the contract term, introducing significant quarter-to-quarter variability in the licensing line that can obscure the underlying royalty trajectory. Child addressed this directly in Q2 FY26: "License revenue in any given quarter reflects the timing of large strategic agreements. When you see a very high licensing quarter, that is often the front-loading of a multi-year economic relationship. The royalty line is the smoother, more predictable indicator of business momentum."

## The Acceleration: Q3 FY26

| Quarter | Total Revenue | Royalty | Licensing | Key Metric |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q3 FY25 | ~$983M | ~$580M | ~$403M | Data center royalty differential confirmed |
| Q4 FY25 | ~$1.24B | ~$760M | ~$480M | Armv9 crosses 30% of royalties |
| Q1 FY26 | ~$1.02B | ~$620M | ~$400M | CSS pipeline at 19 licenses |
| Q2 FY26 | ~$1.05B | ~$650M | ~$400M | 5 CSS customers shipping |
| Q3 FY26 | ~$1.37B | ~$690M | ~$680M | Data center royalties sharply accelerate |
| Q4 FY26 | $1.49B | $671M | $819M | Data center royalties doubled YoY |

The October–December 2025 quarter marked Arm's largest revenue print to that point, extending the Q4 FY25 record. The defining metric for Q3 FY26 was the data center royalty acceleration as Amazon's Graviton-based capacity deployment translated into royalty recognition at scale. AWS reported that the majority of compute capacity added to its fleet in 2025 was Graviton-powered, with its custom silicon business running at more than $20 billion annually and growing triple digits. Even Arm's royalty fraction on each Graviton chip, applied to that volume, generated a royalty pool that moved the aggregate data center line in ways that prior quarters had only suggested.

Guidance accuracy through these four quarters was notably disciplined. Against full-year FY26 guidance of approximately $4.7 to $4.8 billion issued at fiscal year-start, Arm delivered $4.92 billion—a beat of roughly $150 to $200 million at the top end. Child attributed the consistent pattern of conservative guidance to the structural difficulty of predicting large licensing agreement timing: "We can model the royalty side with reasonable precision because we have chip shipment data from our licensees on a lag. The licensing side is harder—a deal that closes in January versus April changes the quarterly print significantly."

## The Silicon Pivot: AGI CPU and the May 6 Earnings Call

The final chapter of fiscal 2026 compressed two seismic events into six weeks. On March 24, 2026, Arm announced the AGI CPU—its first internally designed physical silicon product after 35-plus years as a pure IP licensor. The 3nm data center processor, built on the Neoverse V3 architecture with Meta as the lead development partner, launched with $2 billion in committed customer demand across fiscal years 2027 and 2028, and Haas projected the product line could ultimately reach $15 billion in annual revenue. Six days later, on March 30, Arm and SoftBank jointly published a $25 billion revenue roadmap, setting a roughly 5x expansion ambition from the FY26 base through a combination of Armv9 royalty mix-shift, CSS adoption at scale, data center share gains, and AGI CPU silicon economics.

Q4 FY26 earnings, reported May 6, 2026, confirmed the largest single quarter in Arm's history: $1.49 billion in total revenue, with a record $819 million licensing quarter—reflecting recognition of large CSS agreements signed in the months surrounding the AGI CPU launch—and $671 million in royalties. Data center royalty revenue more than doubled year-over-year, the single most significant metric of the quarter. Full-year FY26 non-GAAP EPS reached a record $1.77 on revenue of $4.92 billion.

On the May 6 call, analyst scrutiny concentrated on the channel relationship between Arm's silicon product and its existing licensee base. Several hyperscalers committed to buying AGI CPU capacity simultaneously hold Arm architecture licenses for their own custom silicon programs—a structural tension that carried implications for the licensing franchise's long-term pricing power. Haas addressed it directly:

> "The way we think about it: the AGI CPU serves customers who want to buy a rack, not design a chip. These are two different buying motions. A company that wants to buy rack capacity and a company that wants to license IP to build their own chip are not the same customer. We think there is room for both, and the data supports that—our CSS license count is still growing even as we announce AGI CPU commitments."

The follow-on analyst concern was forward revenue visibility. Child offered Q1 FY27 guidance of $1.26 billion plus or minus $50 million—implying 20 to 25 percent year-over-year growth—while declining to provide intermediate milestones on the path to $25 billion, citing licensing agreement timing uncertainty. The market's own answer to the visibility question arrived in the price action: Arm shares rose approximately 71 percent in the six weeks following the AGI CPU announcement, a repricing that reflected not the royalty story analysts already knew but the silicon product optionality they were still learning to value.

chapters.title: Rene Haas and the Executive Team: Building the Architect's Ambition
chapters.body:
## The Architect's Instinct

When SoftBank removed Simon Segars as Arm's chief executive in February 2022, the company was weeks away from formally abandoning a $66 billion sale to Nvidia — a deal that had consumed the better part of two years and ended with regulators on three continents concluding that a Nvidia-owned Arm would distort the global semiconductor supply chain. Into that vacancy stepped Rene Haas, then 56 and already four years into leading Arm's IP Products Group, the revenue engine of a company whose every commercial instinct had, until then, been calibrated for the licensing economics of the mobile era.

What separated Haas from the archetypal licensing executive was seven years spent at Nvidia during the period — roughly 2006 to 2013 — when Jensen Huang was constructing the architectural case for the GPU as a platform rather than a graphics accelerator. As Vice President and General Manager of Nvidia's computing products business group, Haas watched a company whose silicon had been relegated to a single workload build CUDA into a software moat so deep that it effectively locked scientific computing, and eventually AI training, into one vendor's ecosystem. The lesson was not lost on him. When he returned to Arm and eventually ascended to the chief executive role, his strategic instinct was to apply the same logic to the CPU world: make the architecture indispensable not just to the chip designer but to every layer of the stack above it, then charge accordingly for that indispensability. [Arm Holdings IR / Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rene_Haas)

The three decisions that define Haas's tenure to date each reflect that conviction. The first was the commercial acceleration of Armv9. The ninth-generation architecture, introduced in 2021, had been positioned as a technical refresh; Haas converted it into a royalty-rate inflection. Armv9's mandatory Scalable Vector Extension and Confidential Compute Architecture frameworks gave every downstream chip designer a genuine engineering reason to migrate from Armv8, and Arm the commercial rationale to charge roughly double the per-unit royalty. By the fourth quarter of fiscal 2025, Armv9-based royalties had crossed 30 percent of total royalty income — a mix-shift milestone that, compounded across a global installed base of tens of billions of chips, represents one of the most significant margin-expansion mechanisms in the company's history.

The second decision was greenlighting Compute Subsystems as a commercial product category. Rather than licensing individual cores and leaving integration engineering to the customer, Arm began delivering fully pre-validated subsystem blueprints that a chip designer could take directly to a foundry. The product commanded approximately double the royalty rate of a standalone core license, and by April 2026 Arm had signed 21 CSS licenses across 12 companies, with five customers already shipping CSS-based chips — including Samsung's Exynos series, which made every major Android phone vendor a CSS-powered device. [Arm Holdings snapshot, April 2026]

The third, and most consequential, was the AGI CPU. Arm's announcement in March 2026 that it had developed its first internally designed physical silicon product — a 3-nanometer data center processor optimized for agentic AI workloads, with Meta as lead development partner and committed demand exceeding $2 billion across fiscal 2027 and 2028 — dissolved the company's 35-year identity as a pure IP licensor. Haas had approved a venture that put Arm in direct competition with the customers it depended on for royalty income, a tension he had presumably modeled during years observing Nvidia navigate its own ecosystem complexities. Whether the wager proves correct will be answered over the next several fiscal years; what is unambiguous is that it could not have been made without a chief executive whose frame of reference extended well beyond the licensing contract.

## The Dual Mandate and Its Discontents

On April 21, 2026, SoftBank Group announced that Haas would assume the additional role of Chief Executive Officer of SoftBank Group International, effective immediately, while retaining the Arm chief executive title. [SoftBank press release, April 21, 2026](https://group.softbank/en/news/press/20260421) The appointment was framed as recognition of his standing as a global technology executive, and Haas had been building the external profile to support it — joining AstraZeneca's board as a Non-Executive Director in January 2025, in addition to his Arm board seat.

The governance question the dual role raises is not subtle. Arm's minority shareholders — holding approximately 10.1 percent of the outstanding equity following the September 2023 Nasdaq IPO — are now led by a chief executive whose second principal is the entity that controls 89.9 percent of their company. [Arm Holdings 20-F FY2026] The structural tension is obvious: when Arm faces a capital allocation decision where SoftBank's preferences diverge from minority shareholders' interests — an acquisition, a dividend policy, an intercompany arrangement — Haas sits on both sides of the table. The 20-F risk factors acknowledge SoftBank's dominance over shareholder votes and the potential for conflicts, but the disclosure of specific governance safeguards protecting minority shareholders from the dual-CEO arrangement is limited. No independent lead director appointment has been publicly announced in connection with the SBGI role. Analysts covering Arm's governance have noted the absence of a formal time-allocation disclosure — how many hours per week Haas commits to each role and whether SBGI work is compensated by SoftBank separately or subsumed in his Arm package.

## Jason Child and the Capital Markets Architecture

Jason Child arrived as Arm's Chief Financial Officer in September 2022, fourteen months before the company's Nasdaq listing. [Arm newsroom, September 2022](https://newsroom.arm.com/news/arm-announces-new-board-members-and-new-chief-financial-officer) His selection reflected the specific demands of preparing a company controlled by a private Japanese conglomerate for American public markets.

Child's prior experience spanned three distinct capital markets environments. At Amazon, where he spent more than eleven years and served as CFO of Amazon International, he operated inside the financial infrastructure of the most complex global retailer-turned-technology company of the internet era, managing currency exposure, transfer pricing, and investor relations across a business with both retail economics and cloud ambitions. At Groupon, he served as CFO through the company's 2011 IPO — one of the more scrutinized technology offerings of that year, which required him to manage disclosure of a non-GAAP metric controversy while guiding the company through its public debut. At Splunk, where he served as CFO prior to the Cisco acquisition, he navigated the translation of an enterprise software business to recurring revenue metrics under institutional investor scrutiny.

The Arm IPO in September 2023 was the largest technology offering of the year, raising $5.23 billion and valuing the company at approximately $54.5 billion at pricing. Child's task was to present a licensing and royalty business — with revenue concentrated in mobile, governed by contracts whose terms were not fully disclosed, and controlled by a shareholder whose own financial situation made the IPO's timing partly exogenous — as a credible growth investment for long-duration technology funds. The $25 billion revenue roadmap that Arm and SoftBank jointly presented in March 2026 is recognizably a Child-era capital markets product: a multi-year framework designed to anchor analyst models and institutional conviction around a specific destination, giving investors a narrative scaffold even as near-term royalty volatility remains tied to smartphone and server chip cycles.

## Board Architecture and the Independence Question

Arm's board of directors, as disclosed in the FY2026 annual report, reflects the reality of 89.9 percent concentrated ownership in a way that diverges from standard large-cap Nasdaq governance norms. SoftBank-nominated directors hold multiple seats, and the company's filing acknowledges that SoftBank, acting alone, can approve or block virtually any shareholder resolution requiring a simple majority. The audit and compensation committees include independent directors, but the board as a whole is not majority-independent by the standard applied to widely held companies, because the majority shareholder's ability to nominate directors means independence in practice is constrained by the controlling shareholder's preferences.

## Segars, the Transition, and Continuity Risk

The circumstances of Simon Segars's departure in February 2022 remain incompletely disclosed. Arm described the change as a board-initiated transition; Segars has not publicly elaborated. The timing — simultaneous with the final stages of the Nvidia deal's regulatory collapse — invites inference, but the disclosed facts do not support specific conclusions about causation. What is material for any assessment of management continuity is that Haas had spent four years inside the IP Products division before his elevation, making him an operational rather than external successor. The institutional knowledge disruption associated with an external CEO hire was avoided, but the concentrated governance that enabled the quick transition is the same concentrated governance that creates the conflict-of-interest risk described above.

## The Retention Calculus

Arm's engineers are among the most sought-after talent in the semiconductor industry. Apple's custom core team in Austin, Nvidia's CPU architecture group building Grace and Vera, Google's CPU Silicon team behind Axion, and Amazon's Annapurna Labs designing Graviton have all recruited from Arm's Cambridge and San Jose campuses. The 2023 IPO created paper wealth for employees who held pre-IPO equity, but it also initiated vesting schedules that, for many engineers, reach their terminal milestones across 2025 to 2027 — precisely the window during which Arm is executing its most technically ambitious programs. The AGI CPU program, Neoverse V3, and the next CSS generation all require deep architectural expertise that takes years to develop and, once liquid, can be monetized at competitors offering substantially richer total compensation. The 20-F risk factors identify key-person concentration as a material risk without naming specific individuals, a disclosure convention that understates the operational reality of a company whose competitive position rests on a relatively small number of CPU architects whose work is not easily or quickly replicated.

chapters.title: The Licensee Ecosystem: From Apple and Qualcomm to Hyperscalers and the AGI CPU Partners
chapters.body:
Arm's revenue model is built on a paradox of ubiquity: the company licenses intellectual property that ships in roughly 30 billion chips per year, yet its commercial fate rests on a handful of relationships with semiconductor designers whose strategic priorities can shift within a single product cycle. Understanding the licensee ecosystem requires mapping five distinct customer segments — mobile OEM and SoC vendors, hyperscaler custom silicon programs, AI infrastructure players, automotive and industrial suppliers, and IoT and embedded chip designers — each with different royalty economics, different growth trajectories, and different strategic dependencies on Arm's continued architectural leadership.

## The Mobile Tier: Apple at the Apex

Apple has been Arm's most commercially significant licensee since the original iPhone launched in 2007 on an Arm application processor, and that relationship deepened across every product generation. Apple holds an architectural license — the highest tier of Arm's licensing hierarchy, granting the right to design custom CPU microarchitectures that implement the Arm instruction set rather than using Arm's reference cores — a status shared with only a handful of chip designers globally. The A-series SoCs powering iPhone and the M-series chips anchoring Mac and iPad are built on Armv9-based custom cores, making Apple the largest volume driver of Armv9 royalty income in mobile.

Arm's [Form 20-F for fiscal 2026](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001973239/000197323926000097/arm-20260331.htm) disclosed, consistent with prior annual filings, that a small number of customers account for a disproportionate share of total revenue, and Apple's status as the single largest licensee has been a fixture of those disclosures. Specific contractual terms and royalty rates are not disclosed. The concentration risk is structural: architectural licenses must be periodically renewed, and Apple's scale means that even modest shifts in royalty rate translate into meaningful dollar impacts on Arm's royalty line. The relationship has held through multiple licensing cycles, and Apple's continued investment in custom Arm silicon for its highest-margin products aligns the two companies' economic interests over any plausible medium-term horizon.

Qualcomm, MediaTek, and Samsung round out the mobile tier. Qualcomm's Snapdragon platform deploys the Oryon CPU core in flagship devices and has expanded into Windows-on-Arm PCs, a market where Arm collects royalties against higher average selling prices than smartphone SoCs. MediaTek's Dimensity series addresses the mid-range Android segment in high volumes across Southeast Asia and China. Samsung was among the first Android OEMs to adopt Arm's Compute Subsystems product, shipping CSS-integrated Exynos chips that pay CSS royalty rates approximately double those of standalone core licenses — an early proof point for the CSS economics thesis that Arm management cited repeatedly through fiscal 2026.

## Hyperscalers: The Data Center Inflection

If mobile defined Arm's first three decades, the data center is defining its fourth. The four major cloud providers — Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and Nvidia — each made material architectural commitments to custom Arm silicon by fiscal year 2026, and the resulting royalty concentration in cloud infrastructure represents the highest-ASP, fastest-growing segment in Arm's royalty pool.

Amazon Web Services' Graviton program became the most commercially significant Arm data center deployment by a substantial margin. AWS disclosed that the majority of compute capacity added to its fleet in calendar year 2025 was Graviton-powered, with the custom silicon business running at more than $20 billion annually and growing at triple-digit rates. Because Graviton chips are priced into AWS instance types carrying higher selling prices than commodity x86 instances — and because Arm collects royalties calculated as a percentage of chip ASP — revenue per chip shipped in the Graviton lineage significantly exceeds that of mobile SoCs.

Google Cloud's Axion processor, built on the Neoverse architecture, had crossed 30,000 migrated cloud applications by early fiscal 2026, capturing both internal Google workloads and third-party developer migration. Microsoft's Cobalt 100 reached 29 global Azure regions, underpinning compute instances available across Microsoft's full commercial footprint. Nvidia's Grace CPU and the successor Vera chip — both Arm-based — served as the CPU pairing for Nvidia's AI server rack architectures, embedding Arm architecture as the CPU layer in the dominant AI infrastructure platform.
